reference_group.label: Adults, pooled
reference_group.description: One provisional range for all adults. No group-specific ranges ship until licensed studies are chosen.
reference_group.note: Development placeholders. These ranges are rounded from commonly taught proportion figures and have not been checked against a licensed anthropometric study, a defined sample, or this build's camera-mesh measurement method. They exist so the report can be built and tested end to end. Replace them before any real user sees a band (spec open question 1; docs/DECISIONS.md D-004).

opener.title: What these numbers can and cannot tell you
can: How specific distances and angles on your face compare with each other, measured the same way every time.
Where each measurement sits against a reference range, and how sure the system is.
Whether a measurement has changed between two scans by more than measurement noise.
cannot: How you look to other people. No measurement here has been shown to predict that, and this report gives no overall score.
Whether anything needs to change. A value outside a range is less common, not worse.
Anything about your health. This is not a medical assessment.
opener.asymmetry: Every face is asymmetric. Most measured asymmetry is normal and is not noticeable to other people.
opener.ranges: Reference ranges describe how a group of people measured. They are population averages, not targets.

face.width_height_ratio

metrics.title: Middle to lower third
metrics.confidence_reason: Repeat measurements on this frame varied by about 1% of the reference range.
metrics.what: The height from your brow line to the base of your nose, divided by the height from the base of your nose to your chin.
metrics.meaning: Your middle and lower thirds are close in height, as they are for most adults.
metrics.definition: (glabella to subnasale) / (subnasale to menton), vertical distances

metrics.title: Space between the eyes
metrics.confidence_reason: Repeat measurements on this frame varied by about 1% of the reference range.
metrics.what: The distance between the inner corners of your eyes as a share of the width of your face at the cheekbones.
metrics.meaning: The space between your eyes takes up a typical share of your face width.

metrics.title: Eye width
metrics.confidence_reason: Repeat measurements on this frame varied by about 1% of the reference range.
metrics.what: The average width of your eye openings, corner to corner, as a share of the width of your face at the cheekbones.
metrics.meaning: Your eye openings take up a typical share of your face width.
metrics.definition: mean palpebral fissure width / bizygomatic width

metrics.title: Face width to height
metrics.confidence_reason: Repeat measurements on this frame varied by about 1% of the reference range.
metrics.what: The width of your face at the cheekbones divided by its height from the bridge of your nose to your chin.
metrics.meaning: The width and height of your face are in a typical relationship.

metrics.title: Canthal tilt
metrics.confidence_reason: Repeat measurements on this frame varied by about 3% of the reference range.
metrics.what: The angle of the line from the inner corner to the outer corner of each eye, averaged over both eyes. A positive value means the outer corner sits higher.
metrics.meaning: Your outer eye corners sit slightly higher than the inner corners, which is the most common arrangement.
metrics.definition: arctan((y_en - y_ex) / (x_ex - x_en)) in image axes, mean of both eyes

metrics.title: Eye spacing
metrics.confidence_reason: Repeat measurements on this frame varied by about 2% of the reference range.
metrics.what: The distance between the inner corners of your eyes divided by the average width of one eye opening.
metrics.meaning: The gap between your eyes is close to the width of one eye, which is typical.
metrics.definition: intercanthal width / mean palpebral fissure width

metrics.title: Eye opening shape
metrics.confidence_reason: Repeat measurements on this frame varied by about 2% of the reference range.
metrics.what: The height of your eye opening divided by its width, averaged over both eyes. Higher values mean a rounder opening, lower values a more elongated one.
metrics.meaning: Your eye openings are more elongated than is typical. Squinting or bright light at capture lowers this reading.
metrics.definition: palpebral fissure height / width, mean of both eyes

metrics.title: Nose width to eye spacing
metrics.confidence_reason: Repeat measurements on this frame varied by about 1% of the reference range.
metrics.what: The width of your nose at the nostrils divided by the distance between the inner corners of your eyes.
metrics.meaning: The width of your nose is close to the space between your eyes, which is typical.

metrics.title: Nasofrontal angle
metrics.confidence_reason: Experimental reading from the 3D mesh, not a validated measurement.
metrics.what: The angle at the bridge of your nose between your brow and your nose tip, seen from the side. Smaller values mean a deeper bridge.
metrics.meaning: Experimental reading. It is estimated from a turned view through a 3D mesh that smooths the outline of the nose and chin, so it is shown without a reference range.
metrics.definition: angle glabella-nasion-pronasale in the sagittal plane

metrics.title: Nasolabial angle
metrics.confidence_reason: Experimental reading from the 3D mesh, not a validated measurement.
metrics.what: The angle at the base of your nose between the underside of your nose and your upper lip, seen from the side.
metrics.meaning: Experimental reading. It is estimated from a turned view through a 3D mesh that smooths the outline of the nose and chin, so it is shown without a reference range.
metrics.definition: angle columella-subnasale-labrale superius in the sagittal plane

metrics.title: Upper to lower lip
metrics.confidence_reason: Repeat measurements on this frame varied by about 2% of the reference range.
metrics.what: The height of your upper lip divided by the height of your lower lip, measured at the centre of your mouth.
metrics.meaning: Your lower lip is fuller, relative to your upper lip, than is typical.
metrics.definition: upper vermilion height / lower vermilion height

metrics.title: Mouth width to nose width
metrics.confidence_reason: Repeat measurements on this frame varied by about 1% of the reference range.
metrics.what: The width of your mouth, corner to corner, divided by the width of your nose at the nostrils.
metrics.meaning: Your mouth is about one and a half times the width of your nose, which is typical.
metrics.definition: mouth width (cheilion to cheilion) / alar width

metrics.title: Philtrum length
metrics.confidence_reason: Repeat measurements on this frame varied by about 3% of the reference range.
metrics.what: The distance from the base of your nose to the top edge of your upper lip, as a fraction of the distance between your pupils.
metrics.meaning: The space between your nose and upper lip is a typical length.
metrics.definition: subnasale to labrale superius, vertical, in IPD units

metrics.title: Jaw angle
metrics.confidence_reason: Experimental reading from the 3D mesh, not a validated measurement.
metrics.what: The angle at the corner of your jaw between the back edge of the jaw and its lower edge, seen from the side.
metrics.meaning: Experimental reading. It is estimated from a turned view through a 3D mesh that smooths the outline of the nose and chin, so it is shown without a reference range.
metrics.definition: angle zygion-gonion-menton on the camera-facing side, sagittal plane

metrics.title: Jaw width to cheekbone width
metrics.confidence_reason: Repeat measurements on this frame varied by about 0% of the reference range.
metrics.what: The width of your jaw at its corners divided by the width of your face at the cheekbones.
metrics.meaning: Your jaw width and cheekbone width are in a typical relationship.

metrics.title: Chin projection
metrics.confidence_reason: Experimental reading from the 3D mesh, not a validated measurement.
metrics.what: How far the front of your chin sits in front of or behind the base of your nose, seen from the side, as a fraction of the distance between your pupils. Negative means behind.
metrics.meaning: Experimental reading. It is estimated from a turned view through a 3D mesh that smooths the outline of the nose and chin, so it is shown without a reference range.
metrics.definition: pogonion depth minus subnasale depth, in IPD units

face_shape.label: oval
face_shape.text: Your face is somewhat longer than it is wide, with a jaw a little narrower than your cheekbones. Face shape is a styling convention, not a measurement standard, and many faces sit between two shapes.

overall.title: Overall symmetry index
overall.confidence_reason: Repeat measurements on this frame varied by about 0.0% of the value.
overall.what: How closely the left and right halves of your face mirror each other across the midline. 1.000 would be an exact mirror image, which no real face is.
overall.meaning: Every face has some left-right difference, and most measured asymmetry is normal. A slight head turn or uneven lighting at capture also lowers this reading.

symmetry.note: Brighter marks show where the left and right sides differ most. Mild asymmetry is normal: every face has it, and most of it is not noticeable to other people.

skin.reason: The synthetic sample has no photo, so there is no skin to assess.
skin.note: Experimental. These bands come from simple image statistics, not a trained skin model. They shift with lighting and camera, and they have not been validated across skin tones.

summary.text: Of the 12 proportions compared with a reference range, 10 sit within the typical range. More distinctive for you are eye opening shape (0.26, below the range) and upper to lower lip (0.45, below the range). Distinctive means less common in the reference group; it does not mean better or worse. Your overall symmetry index is 0.993. Every face has some left-right difference, and most measured asymmetry is normal. The reference ranges in this build are provisional placeholders, so treat each band as a rough guide.

plan.preface: Proportions such as facial thirds or jaw width come from bone structure. No routine changes them, and this plan does not try to. It covers skin, grooming and habits, in order of how good the evidence is for each.

items.action: If you smoke, stopping is the largest change you can make for your skin
items.detail: Smoking speeds up wrinkling and dulls skin tone. Your doctor or pharmacist can help with quitting.
items.reason: Suggested because it matches your skin goal.
items.evidence_note: Large observational and twin studies link smoking to faster skin ageing.

items.action: Keep a regular sleep schedule of 7 to 9 hours
items.detail: Short sleep makes the under-eye area look darker and puffier the next day. Regular sleep is the first thing to try for under-eye darkness.
items.evidence_note: Controlled studies link sleep loss to darker under-eye appearance.

items.action: Wear broad-spectrum sunscreen, SPF 30 or higher, every day
items.detail: Apply to face and neck each morning and reapply when outdoors. This is the single habit with the best evidence for slowing visible skin ageing and uneven pigmentation.
items.reason: Suggested because it matches your skin goal.
items.evidence_note: Randomised trials show daily use slows photoageing.

items.action: Cleanse gently and moisturise once or twice a day
items.detail: A mild, fragrance-free cleanser and a plain moisturiser support the skin barrier, which evens out the look of texture and dryness. Harsh scrubs tend to make texture and redness more visible.
items.reason: Suggested because it matches your skin goal.
items.evidence_note: Trials show moisturisers improve barrier function and roughness.

items.detail: Retinoids are the best-studied ingredient class for skin texture and fine lines. Start two or three nights a week, use sunscreen in the morning, and expect dryness at first. Do not use them if you are pregnant or trying to conceive; ask a pharmacist if unsure.
items.reason: Suggested because it matches your skin goal.
items.evidence_note: Strong trial evidence for prescription strengths; moderate for retinol.

items.action: If you grow facial hair, shape it to follow your jaw line
items.detail: A clean neckline and cheek line frame the lower face. A barber can set the lines for you to maintain.
items.reason: Suggested because it matches your style goal.

items.detail: Removing stray hairs between and below the brows keeps their natural shape clear. Avoid reshaping heavily, since over-plucked brows can be slow to grow back.
items.reason: Suggested because it matches your style goal.

items.action: Ask a barber or stylist for a cut that suits your face shape
items.detail: Take your face-shape result with you. Volume and length can change how wide or long a face reads. The full style guide arrives in a later release.
items.reason: Suggested because it matches your style goal.

items.category_label: Topics to discuss with a professional
items.action: Have any new or changing spot checked by a doctor
items.detail: This app looks at overall tone only. It cannot assess moles or skin lesions. See a doctor about any spot that is new, changing, itchy or bleeding.
items.reason: Suggested because it matches your skin goal.

items.category_label: Topics to discuss with a professional
items.action: If you are considering any procedure, take these questions
items.detail: Questions to ask: is the provider board-certified in the relevant specialty, how often do they perform this, what is the realistic range of outcomes including poor ones, what are the risks, the recovery and the cost of revision, and what happens if I do nothing? This report cannot tell you whether a procedure is right for you.
